Continual learning systems must update a model sequentially on new task distributions without destroying performance on prior tasks — the core tension is that gradient updates optimizing for new data move model parameters into regions that corrupt previously learned representations. The embedding space is where this damage is most legible: what looks like stable accuracy on a held-out task can mask severe geometric distortion in how the model clusters and separates concepts, distortion that only surfaces when the model encounters compositional or out-of-distribution inputs. Replay buffers — storing exemplars from prior tasks to interleave with new training — are the standard mitigation, but heterogeneous composition (buffers mixing tasks with different class densities, feature statistics, or label granularities) introduces a subtler problem: the replay distribution doesn't match any real task distribution, so the model is perpetually optimizing against a synthetic mixture that can warp the embedding manifold in ways no single task would. An expert worries specifically about interference geometry — the angle and magnitude of conflicting gradients from heterogeneous replay batches — because two replay samples that individually produce reasonable updates can jointly push a shared representation in directions that satisfy neither task, producing embeddings that are metrically incoherent: nearby points in embedding space no longer share meaningful semantic structure.

Beginners fixate on forgetting as measured by accuracy drop; experts watch for representational drift without accuracy collapse, where the model appears to perform adequately on benchmark metrics while the underlying embedding geometry degrades silently, making the system brittle to any downstream use — retrieval, transfer, or zero-shot generalization — that depends on the manifold structure rather than just the classification boundary.

The cleanest diagnostic is to freeze the head and probe the backbone on held-out exemplars from prior tasks: healthy adaptation produces a backbone whose frozen embeddings remain linearly separable for old tasks (a linear probe trained in 10-20 gradient steps recovers >90% of original accuracy), while pathological masking reveals itself when the frozen backbone fails the linear probe even though end-to-end accuracy was intact — the head had learned a contorted decision boundary compensating for incoherent features. A second signal is head weight norm growth per task: in pathological masking, head weights for old classes tend to grow in magnitude over time as the head strains to separate geometrically interpenetrating embeddings; Caccia et al. (2022) in their analysis of "New Insights on Reducing Abrupt Representation Change in Online Continual Learning" document exactly this pattern, showing that representation change rates correlate with downstream head weight inflation. A third concrete test — borrowed from the mechanistic interpretability toolkit — is to measure the condition number of the Jacobian of the head's output with respect to the backbone's final-layer activations: a well-adapted head over a coherent manifold has a low-condition-number Jacobian (output varies smoothly and proportionally to input); a masking head has a high condition number, meaning tiny moves in embedding space cause large swings in logits, a signature of the head fighting the geometry. The distinction sharply changes intervention: healthy adaptation warrants leaving the head free and possibly using representation regularization on the backbone only (e.g., feature distillation losses as in PODNet, Douillard et al. 2020, which penalize changes to intermediate feature maps); pathological masking instead calls for resetting and retraining the head periodically from frozen backbone embeddings — a strategy validated in SLDA (streaming linear discriminant analysis heads over fixed or slowly-drifting backbones) — combined with aggressive geometric regularization like manifold mixup in the replay buffer to restore cluster structure before the head sees it.

The strongest training-time constraint is gradient projection onto a task-specific null space: before applying any backbone update, project the gradient so it has zero component in the directions that matter for prior task embeddings — this is the core idea in OWM (Orthogonal Weights Modification, Zeng et al. 2019) and GPM (Gradient Projection Memory, Saha et al. 2021), where GPM explicitly maintains a basis of "important directions" per task via SVD of activation matrices and achieves near-zero backward transfer interference on Split-CIFAR100 while keeping embeddings linearly separable. The architectural complement is embedding space normalization with a fixed-radius hypersphere constraint — enforcing that all embeddings live on a unit hypersphere (via L2 normalization of the backbone output) before the head, as in SupCon-style losses (Khosla et al. 2020); this eliminates norm-based degrees of freedom the backbone would otherwise exploit to "hide" task interference in magnitude rather than direction, keeping geometric structure legible. A third concrete mechanism is per-task feature statistics anchoring via batch normalization freezing or task-conditioned BN: in continual learning, shared BN layers are a primary vector for feature statistic corruption across heterogeneous tasks, and approaches like CN-DPM and more directly the work of Pham et al. (2021) in "Continual Normalization" show that freezing or conditionally routing BN statistics per task reduces representational drift measurably — on Split-MiniImageNet, task-conditioned normalization recovered ~4-6% linear probe accuracy compared to shared BN under the same replay budget. Perhaps most underappreciated is contrastive replay objectives applied directly in embedding space rather than cross-entropy on logits: if the backbone is trained to maintain inter-class distances in the embedding space explicitly (not just get classification right), the loss function directly penalizes the geometric corruption you're trying to prevent, rather than only caring about decision boundaries — Co²L (Cha et al. 2021) demonstrates this produces more stable linear separability under heterogeneous replay than distillation-only baselines, with roughly 3-5% better linear probe retention on class-incremental benchmarks.

The bias propagates through a precise mechanism: GPM constructs its subspace basis via SVD of the activation matrix A where rows are per-exemplar activations, so if the replay buffer overrepresents certain feature clusters (e.g., tasks with larger class counts or higher visual diversity dominate the buffer), the top singular vectors capture those clusters' directions disproportionately, and the resulting projection nullspace incorrectly treats directions important for underrepresented tasks as "free" — meaning gradients for new tasks are allowed to move freely in exactly those directions, producing targeted forgetting of the underrepresented tasks while appearing to protect the dominant ones. This becomes actively harmful — not just suboptimal — when the biased subspace estimate is positively misleading: if two tasks share a similar activation direction but with different semantic content (a common occurrence in heterogeneous buffers where, say, texture-biased and shape-biased tasks coexist), GPM conflates them into a single protected direction, and the projection then blocks gradient updates that would actually be beneficial for the new task and for the underrepresented prior task, creating a frozen-but-wrong subspace that degrades all three simultaneously. Saha et al. acknowledge in the GPM paper that subspace quality degrades with fewer exemplars but don't fully analyze the heterogeneous-composition case; subsequent work by Deng et al. (2021) in "Flattening Sharpness for Dynamic Gradient Projection" shows empirically that projection under poor subspace estimates can produce loss landscape sharpening — the model finds narrow minima that satisfy the projection constraint but generalize worse, measurable as a 2-4x increase in Hessian trace compared to unprojected training on the same tasks. A concrete failure mode to watch for is subspace dimensionality inflation: when buffer composition is heterogeneous, the activation matrix has high effective rank (many directions look "important" because they're important for different tasks in the mixture), so GPM expands the protected subspace to cover them all, eventually protecting so many directions that the remaining nullspace is too small to accommodate new task learning — the system effectively freezes, and new task accuracy plateaus or collapses, which looks superficially like catastrophic forgetting but has the opposite cause. The intervention this demands is importance-weighted SVD where exemplar contributions to the activation matrix are reweighted inversely proportional to their task's buffer representation frequency before decomposition — this corrects the sampling bias at the source rather than downstream — though to my knowledge this specific correction hasn't been cleanly validated in a published continual learning paper, representing a concrete open implementation gap.

The principled framing is to treat subspace eviction as a resource allocation problem with an explicit forgetting budget, where you're choosing not "which task to forget" but "which task's forgetting costs least given current system state" — this requires three quantities per task: the volume of subspace it currently occupies (measured as number of singular vectors above a threshold), the sensitivity of its performance to losing those directions (measurable via a quick linear probe accuracy drop test after hypothetically zeroing those vectors), and its recoverability via replay (tasks with richer replay buffer representation can tolerate subspace eviction because the buffer will partially reconstruct the lost geometry through future gradient updates). The most defensible eviction criterion combining these is forgetting-per-dimension: evict the task whose (projected accuracy loss) / (subspace dimensions freed) ratio is smallest, prioritizing tasks where you buy back many dimensions at low accuracy cost — this is structurally analogous to the page eviction policies in operating systems memory management, and Chaudhry et al.'s A-GEM (2019) implicitly gestures at this by weighting constraint violations by task frequency, though it doesn't formalize dimension-level accounting. A critical complication is that sensitivity estimates are interdependent: evicting task A's subspace may shift which directions are critical for task B if their subspaces were partially overlapping, meaning naive greedy eviction produces cascading errors — the correct approach is to estimate the full Jacobian of all task probe accuracies with respect to each candidate eviction, which is expensive but approximable via influence functions (Koh & Liang 2017) applied to the SVD basis rather than individual parameters. Farajtabar et al.'s Orthogonal Gradient Descent (OGD, 2020) provides a related insight: when subspaces overlap, projecting onto the intersection rather than the union recovers shared structure that neither task alone would protect, suggesting that before eviction you should first merge overlapping subspace claims — replacing two partially-redundant task bases with their shared component plus task-specific remainders — which can reduce total protected dimensionality by 20-30% in practice before any true eviction is necessary. The hardest part that no current paper handles cleanly is non-stationarity of task importance: if the system will later be evaluated heavily on an evicted task, that eviction is catastrophic; if that task is never queried again, it's free — and without knowledge of the future query distribution, the principled answer requires either a prior over future task relevance (which must come from the deployment context) or a minimax strategy that minimizes worst-case forgetting across all possible eviction orderings, a formulation that exists theoretically but has no efficient practical implementation in continual learning systems today.

Learning a query-frequency prior online means maintaining a running estimate of task relevance — concretely, a decayed count vector where each query increments that task's weight and an exponential decay (half-life tuned to the expected non-stationarity timescale) down-weights older evidence — then using those weights to bias both subspace eviction decisions and replay buffer sampling proportionally; this is structurally identical to what caching systems like ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache, Megiddo & Modha 2003) do with page access frequencies, and the analogy is tight enough that ARC's provable competitiveness guarantees against optimal offline eviction carry over conceptually, though continual learning adds the complication that "accessing" a task also changes its representation. The first serious failure mode is recency collapse under bursty queries: if the deployment environment sends a long burst of queries for task A followed by silence, the decayed estimator concludes task A is maximally important and evicts subspace for everything else, then when queries shift to task B the system has already destroyed B's geometry — a problem that ARC partially solves via its two-queue structure (recency vs. frequency) but that continual learning systems haven't yet adopted, meaning a single query storm can permanently restructure the forgetting landscape. The adversarial case is more alarming: an adversary who knows the eviction policy can induce targeted forgetting by sending synthetic query bursts for low-value tasks, inflating their apparent importance until the system evicts subspace for high-value tasks the adversary wants degraded — this is a concrete security vulnerability in any deployed continual learning system whose eviction policy is query-adaptive and whose query interface is externally accessible, and to my knowledge no published system has analyzed this attack surface explicitly. A subtler failure mode arises from distribution shift in the query-relevance correlation: the system learns that tasks queried frequently are tasks worth preserving, but this assumes the query pattern is informative about future needs — in non-stationary environments, past query frequency can be negatively correlated with future relevance (e.g., a task is queried heavily during a now-finished project phase and never again), causing the prior to systematically protect stale tasks and evict emerging-importance ones. The mitigation space involves either query-pattern change-point detection (monitoring the query distribution itself for structural breaks and resetting the relevance prior when one is detected, using sequential hypothesis tests like CUSUM) or abandoning the learned prior entirely in favor of importance estimates grounded in downstream loss sensitivity rather than query frequency — measuring how much each task's held-out loss would increase under eviction, which is query-independent but requires periodic evaluation passes that themselves consume compute and may not reflect adversarial query manipulation.

The default policy during the blind window should be eviction suspension with gradient projection freezing — stop all subspace evictions and freeze backbone updates entirely, accepting temporary plasticity loss in exchange for preventing irreversible geometric damage during the period when you have least information to guide forgetting decisions; this is the continual learning analog of a database system entering read-only mode during a transaction log corruption event, prioritizing consistency over availability. The right policy then branches on change-point cause, which the detection system should attempt to classify simultaneously with detection: if the change-point is a distributional shift in query topics (new tasks becoming relevant, detectable via rising query entropy and appearance of out-of-distribution inputs), the correct blind-window policy is to allocate a small protected subspace reserve — dimensions held back from any task's exclusive claim — that can absorb initial gradient updates for the emerging distribution without evicting anything, essentially buying time for the new relevance signal to accumulate. If the change-point is instead a query storm or adversarial injection (sudden spike in query volume for a narrow task slice, detectable via abnormally low query entropy and repetitive input structure), the blind-window policy inverts: maintain the pre-reset prior frozen rather than going fully uninformed, since the pre-reset prior is likely more reliable than any estimate derived from the anomalous burst, and flag the period for human review if the system has that affordance. The duration of the blind window is itself a critical parameter — CUSUM detectors have a configurable average run length (ARL) that trades false positive rate against detection delay, and in practice a well-tuned CUSUM on query distributions detects true shift within 50-200 queries (depending on shift magnitude), meaning the blind window should be budgeted as exactly that length, after which a new prior is reliable enough to resume eviction decisions. The deepest problem is that cause classification and change-point detection are not separable in practice: the same CUSUM statistic that fires for adversarial injection also fires for legitimate distribution shift, and misclassifying the cause leads to the worst possible policy response — freezing updates when you should be adapting, or adapting when you should be freezing — suggesting the blind window policy should be explicitly robust to cause uncertainty, perhaps via a minimax mixture that partially freezes and partially reserves, accepting suboptimality under both hypotheses rather than optimizing hard for either.
